stem.text: The European hedgehog, Erinaceus europaeus, is a small omnivorous mammal. Its body is covered in spines, which are usually brown. A rare variant, which lacks the brown pigment, has blonde (pale yellow) spines. This characteristic is coded for by a recessive allele.
Fig. 1.1 shows a European hedgehog with blonde spines.

stem.caption: Fig. 1.1
stem.alt: Photograph of a European hedgehog with blonde spines.

stem.text: Alderney is a small island between the UK and France. Hedgehogs were not found on Alderney until the 1960s, when three pairs of hedgehogs were introduced to the island. The hedgehogs started to breed and some of the offspring had blonde spines.
By 2017, the population of hedgehogs, including individuals with brown spines and individuals with blonde spines, had increased to approximately 600.
Suggest reasons why the population of hedgehogs increased to such a large number.

points.text: high birth rate / short generation time / AW ;
few / no, predators ;
little competition ;
plenty of food available / wide range of food types eaten / omnivore ;

explanation.text: A newly introduced population can increase when births exceed deaths and resources are sufficient. This ecological inference is attached to the capacity for reproduction, competition and survival in 17.2(1), rather than to a separate population-growth outcome.

reasoningChain: Consider factors affecting births and deaths.
Relate food, competition and predation to the island population.

stem.text: A survey taken in 2017 showed that 60% of the hedgehogs on Alderney had blonde spines.
Suggest and explain reasons why the proportion of hedgehogs with blonde spines was so high.

blonde spines have a selective advantage / described / AW ;
allele frequency for blonde spines increases / increased homozygosity (for recessive or blonde allele) ;
inbreeding ;

explanation.text: Separate a chance change in the founding gene pool from selection after introduction. A recessive phenotype becomes visible in homozygotes, so allele frequency and mating between relatives can affect the proportion observed.

reasoningChain: Distinguish drift from a selective advantage.
Link recessive homozygosity to the visible phenotype.

Explain why it is sometimes important to control invasive alien species.

bullets: Most candidates were able to suggest two or more reasons to explain why the population of hedgehogs on Alderney had increased substantially following their introduction.

Candidates found this question problematic. Many considered that blonde spines could give a selective advantage to hedgehogs although few referred to directional selection by name. A small number of candidates recognised the possibility of genetic drift due to an initially small gene pool (founder effect).

Many candidates recognised the need to control invasive alien species and a variety of valid explanations were suggested. Competition with native species for food (and other resources) and predation on native species were often cited as problems. Other valid explanations recognised that alien species may have no predators to control their numbers or may reproduce more successfully than native species. Some responses correctly noted that the consequence of these problems would be a reduction in biodiversity.
